title: The Monster Natty that trains EVERY DAY (Geoffrey Verity Schofield)
summary: First episode of a lifter-profile series: NH reviews Geoffrey Verity Schofield's six-day RAVAGE program (legs/torso/arms twice a week), praising the exercise selection, leg days and supersets while criticising high rep ranges, back-to-back torso and arm days and token neck/forearm work. He then draws lessons from GVS's methods (taking every set to absolute failure, size not limited by strength) and grades his physique by muscle group.
claims: The first rule of the fitness industry when making a program is to give it a cool name
RAVAGE is a six-day split: legs, torso, arms, legs, torso, arms, Sunday off; a lot of volume and frequency, meant for intermediates
Opening leg day with a hack squat (or Smith hack squat) for 5-10 reps then 10-15 rep backup sets is a good quad-biased start
Good mornings or Romanian deadlifts are preferable to back extensions after a hack squat, since the machine leaves the lower back fresh
The rule of three sets: most exercises are best done for 2-4 sets, so three, which keeps volume and intensity easy to manage
Lunges and split squats are energy and motivation vampires; never open or close leg day with them, third is ideal
Do split squats for 8-12 or 10-15 reps, never 30, or the fatigue is excessive
Leg days should be shorter than upper days because one set of squats does far more than one set of bench
At most one compound and one isolation per leg muscle; one heavy squat plus three quad isolations is junk volume
Pair a press with a pull as a superset whenever possible; it is free volume, but never force supersets that don't fit
The narrow neutral-grip pulldown is the best pulldown for the back
Offering sensible alternatives for each exercise is a strength in a program
GVS's sixth torso exercise (cable pullover) is junk volume for most people and can be cut
Never place upper days and arm days next to each other unless upper days contain no arm isolation; training triceps and delts the day after heavy pressing hurts recovery
Hammer curls for 15-20 reps are too high; 8-12 is better
Rotating exercise variations within a high-frequency program prevents exercise fatigue and supports double progression
Spider curls or preacher curls are better than incline dumbbell curls for training the biceps lengthened
Overhead extensions give a huge long-head stretch; the long head of the triceps responds best to higher reps and endurance
Open leg day with a hip hinge once in a while for better performance on it, unless quads are the priority
Three heavy sets of Romanian deadlifts at RPE 8-9 are all you need; no point doing five plus backups
Most people cannot combine this much frequency and volume and should drop to 3-4 days or fewer sets; on four days keep one leg, one arm and one chest day
Insert a rest day between the torso day and the arm day instead of resting only on Sunday
One set a week of neck and forearm work is not enough and leads to imbalances
Train forearms and neck on leg days, superset with leg lifts, since upper days the next day barely need them
Very high rep ranges everywhere make it hard to control volume and intensity and lead to plateaus where you repeat the same weights; aim for 6-10 or 8-12
Forced partials with body English at the end of a set are free volume; only small people worry about cheating
He trains six days a week but does only 3-4 sets per exercise and very low rep ranges, far less volume than GVS
Machine- and cable-heavy programs allow much more workload with less joint stress than free-weight-only ones
Heavy squats and deadlifts are mostly not the best for hypertrophy
Size and strength ratios differ between people; don't let strength limit your pursuit of size, since the weight on the bar is only a tool for hypertrophy
Going hard means taking every set to absolute failure with total focus on that set alone
GVS is natural; he broke the so-called natural limit that lazy natural YouTubers invented to excuse quitting hard training
If your front is better than your back, it's usually because you trained the front more
GVS has the best triceps long head in natural YouTube fitness because he trains it with intense isolation to failure
A neck should line up with the jawline; big traps and a pencil neck look wrong
Being much stronger on vertical than horizontal presses signals a shoulder-chest imbalance where shoulders steal the work
Strong glutes and lower back can steal hamstring work in hip hinges
GVS needs direct ab isolation; his abs are his weakest point and would tie the physique together
Most people have C-tier calves except some Asians and formerly fat people
exercises: energy vampire; never first or last
